item.title: From funding with own college fees to 1,000+ beds: how oho Living won Tier-2
item.description: oho Living, a Tier-2 managed rental startup, grew revenue 25x after its worst year and now runs 1,032 beds across six cities.
item.content:encoded:
Anyone who has moved to a new city for college or a first job knows the feeling. You arrive with a suitcase and an address you can barely find, and the room you are handed is bare. Nobody tells you where to buy groceries or whom to call when the geyser breaks. You figure it out alone.

In cities like Ranchi, Patna and Jaipur, the choice was usually between expensive premium housing and bare rooms with no standard at all. Students and young professionals who wanted a clean, well-run home at a fair price had nowhere to go, and landlords and young tenants rarely trusted each other.

oho Living was built to fill that gap. It now runs 1,032 beds across six cities, with one promise: to be the friend in the city for everyone who moves to one.

From listings to homes

Ritu Raj had tried to solve this once before. In college, he built GoForRooms, a website that helped students find a place to stay. It could point someone to a room, but it could not promise what living there would be like.

So when he started oho Living, paying for it with his college fees, the team chose to run the homes themselves. It began with a single property in Ranchi, run the way a friend would run it, and grew one property and one city at a time.

The model is simple. oho Living signs an agreement with a property owner, as a lease, a revenue share or a franchise, and takes full responsibility for the resident. The owner no longer manages tenants, and the resident no longer deals with an unpredictable landlord.

The founders

Ritu, now Co-founder and CBO, leads sales and growth. Saurabh Kumar, Co-founder and CEO, owns strategy, brand and fundraising; at 25, he already has more than a decade of startup-building behind him, including a social media community of over 13 million followers. Prakhar Minocha, Co-founder and COO, runs the homes and the teams behind them, drawing on more than nine years in real estate, including a villa rental business and a hotel on Airbnb.

The simplest idea in the room

In 2021, Jharkhand Angels gathered startups from across the state at one event. Most were pitching food delivery, e-commerce, job platforms, even VR. oho Living was solving the plainest problem in the room: helping people find a good place to live.

Then the founders said they wanted to serve 1 crore people, starting from Ranchi. Most of the room laughed. One investor laughed too, then caught himself asking: why not?

The worst year

The early years were a grind. Founders in their early twenties had to convince landlords and institutions to take them seriously, and running homes meant something broke almost every day. The team answered with structure, writing SOPs and playbooks while the company was still small.

That did not prevent 2023, the founders' lowest point. The business had split into two parts, and they could not see the next step. Jharkhand Angels stepped in as an adviser and helped restructure the company.

The bet due diligence said no to

By December 2024, oho Living was steadier, but revenue was still small. Saurabh sat down with the investor and laid out his plan to go big. This time, the vision landed.

Due diligence said no. Jharkhand Angels invested anyway, backing the founders and the Tier-2 thesis over the numbers. The money came in by July 2025.

In the year that followed, monthly revenue rose about 25 times, from roughly ₹2.5 lakh to around ₹50 lakh. Homes went from average to genuinely good, the premium Signature brand launched, a sixth city was added, and EBITDA began to look predictable.

As the investor put it, everyone now calls Tier-2 India the big bet. These founders saw it years earlier.

A Community Manager, not a property manager

For the founders, a resident's experience does not end at the door of their room. Community forms when people feel safe and seen, so every home has a Community Manager instead of a property manager.

Three brands serve three kinds of newcomer: Signature for premium full buildings, Urban for working professionals, and LiveliHood for students, run with education partners including Motion, PhysicsWallah and Allen. Matured properties run at around 95% occupancy.

Growing on partners' money

oho Living's recent growth has come without spending its own capital on property. In Patna, coaching institutes fund student residences and send the students, while oho Living runs them; 512 beds there earned about ₹27 lakh a month from day one. In Jaipur, landlords pay for the fit-out and oho Living pays a fixed rent. In Agra, landlords furnish the flats and share the revenue.

The five deals signed this quarter, including a franchise in progress with Bhubaneswar's Shaswat Group, added 658 beds and ₹57.3 lakh in monthly revenue capacity.

What comes next

The company plans to reach 2,134 beds by March 2027, led by Patna, Jaipur and Bhubaneswar. At 80% occupancy, that would mean about ₹1.49 crore in monthly revenue. Urban is set to become the largest brand as more young professionals move to Tier-2 cities for work.

Beyond that, Vision 2030 is 100,000 beds across every state in India, with a website that lets anyone find a home and move in within 10 minutes.

And the number that made a room laugh in 2021 has not shrunk. Saurabh still talks about serving 1 crore people.

oho Living did not start perfect. In the founders' words, it started honest: a real problem, a small team and a commitment to figure it out along the way. For anyone arriving in a new city with a suitcase and an address they can barely find, that is the point.

item.title: 11,000 applied, 10 made the cut: Meet the UAE-India Start-up Series finalists
item.description: Ten Indian start-ups, picked from 11,000 applicants, pitch in Bengaluru on 18 November for a spot in Hub71’s Abu Dhabi programmes.
item.content:encoded:
More than 11,000 Indian start-ups applied to the second edition of the UAE-India Start-up Series. Ten are left. On the afternoon of 18 November in Bengaluru, each will get seven minutes to argue that its business is ready for the UAE: three minutes to pitch and four to answer questions.

The UAE-India Start-up Series helps Indian start-ups enter and scale in the UAE market. It is anchored in the UAE-India Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), whose start-up provisions call for closer ties between incubators and accelerators in the two countries. Abu Dhabi's technology ecosystem Hub71 is the Series' cross-border partner. Its second edition, the UAE-India Start-up Series 2.0, ends with a two-day Final Pitch Event on 17 and 18 November.

The edition arrives as more Indian founders look to the Gulf for their next market. The UAE offers capital, a route into the wider region and a business culture many Indian companies already know. The harder question, and the one the final will test, is which companies can turn that interest into paying customers there.

From 11,000 applications to ten

The ten finalists come from four sectors: artificial intelligence (three start-ups), energy and climate (three), deep tech and robotics (three) and digital assets (one). They are based across the country, from Bengaluru, Chennai and Pune to Bhubaneswar and West Bengal.

Most are well past the idea stage. Several report revenue in the millions of dollars, and three already sell into the UAE:

  • Onsite counts 59 UAE customers among its 1,591 paying customers.
  • Flo Mobility has robots working on construction sites for ALEC in the UAE.
  • XYMA Analytics has deployed its sensors with Emirates Steel.

The final pitches come after a day and a half of preparation. Finalists will meet investors one-on-one and take part in mentorship and pitch practice. That includes a session led by Hub71 on entering and scaling in the UAE.

The winners will be announced on the night of 18 November, when the Top 50 Investment Dossier will also be released.

The ten finalists

The finalists are listed below in the order they will pitch. Figures are as reported by the companies to the organisers.

# Start-up Sector Founders What it does
1 OnsiteNew Delhi AI Akshansh Agarwal, Sumit Garg, Dheeraj Anand AI-powered construction management software for contractors and developers.
2 PointoWest Bengal Energy and climate Riki Biswas A circular platform that sells, finances, services and refurbishes electric vehicle batteries.
3 CYRAN AINew Delhi Deep tech and robotics Prof. Manan Suri AI that helps aerospace and precision manufacturers catch defects before a part ships.
4 KoinXBhubaneswar Digital assets Punit Agarwal, Guna Shekar Crypto tax and accounting software.
5 NawgatiNoida AI Vaibhav Kaushik, Aryan Sisodia, Aalaap Nair An AI and IoT platform that gives fuel companies a single, real-time view of each station.
6 SustVestGurgaon Energy and climate Hardik Bhatia, Devansh Shah Rooftop solar for businesses at no upfront cost, with fractional ownership for individual investors.
7 EconovusPune Energy and climate Ramesh Prasad Carbon-neutral, wood-free export packaging for carmakers including Skoda-VW, Hyundai and Mahindra.
8 Flo MobilityBengaluru Deep tech and robotics Manesh Jain, Pratik Patel Autonomous robots that move materials across construction sites.
9 XYMA AnalyticsChennai Deep tech and robotics Dr Nishanth Raja, Aswin Kathirvel Ultrasonic sensors that monitor industrial equipment at extreme temperatures.
10 ForthcodeBengaluru AI Ajith Balakumar AI and inflight retail technology that helps airlines earn more from extras such as baggage and seat selection.

What is at stake: a route into Abu Dhabi

The main prize is a place in Hub71's programmes in Abu Dhabi. Hub71 first announced its partnership with the Series in November 2025 and confirmed it for the second edition at its Impact Event in June 2026.

Hub71 Access Programme. Three start-ups will be shortlisted and one will be onboarded. That company gets up to AED 250,000 (about ₹65 lakh) in in-kind incentives and AED 250,000 (about ₹65 lakh) in cash through a SAFE note, an investment that converts into equity at a later funding round. It also receives mentorship, investor introductions, regulatory support and access to Hub71's corporate and government partners.

Hub71 Immersion Programme. Up to six start-ups will spend a week in virtual preparation on the Abu Dhabi and UAE ecosystem. They then spend a week at Hub71 in person, with sessions on market entry and introductions across its partner network. According to the Series website, the UAE leg for selected start-ups begins in March 2027.

What the first edition delivered

The first edition of the Series concluded in New Delhi in 2025, with twenty start-ups pitching in its final. Five of them moved on to Hub71. Endimension, an AI-first radiology platform, joined the Access Programme as part of Cohort 18. BioReform, Docket Run, Data Sutram and SBNRI entered the Immersion Programme.

The second edition has a smaller final and a field that is, on paper, further along. One question to watch is whether the jury backs start-ups that already have UAE customers or those with the most room to grow there. The longer test comes after the event: how many finalists build a lasting presence in the UAE.

item.title: How flexible workspaces are changing the way companies think about offices
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Manish Khedia of The Executive Centre discussed how businesses are moving beyond traditional office layouts and long-term leases to focus on flexibility, collaboration, and employee needs.
item.content:encoded:
The COVID-19 pandemic changed how companies think about offices. After employees spent months working from home, businesses had to reconsider what would bring people back to the workplace and how to make that time productive.

At TechSparks 2026, Manish Khedia, Regional Managing Director at The Executive Centre (TEC), joined Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, for a fireside chat titled ‘The enterprise office 2.0: Space, strategy, experience redefined’.

The discussion covered how flexible workspaces, hybrid working arrangements, and employee expectations are changing the way businesses plan their offices.

From square footage to collaboration

For years, companies made office decisions based largely on location, square footage, the number of workstations, and the type of building. The pandemic changed those priorities, first by forcing employees to work from home and then by making companies reconsider how to bring them back.

According to Khedia, the challenge now is to create offices that employees want to visit, where they can work productively, collaborate, and have access to the facilities they need.

“I think all the companies are looking at how they can engage their employees to be more productive, not by giving them more work, but by creating an environment where they can collaborate,” he said.

As a result, businesses are looking beyond a premium address when choosing office space. They are considering the surrounding infrastructure, including technology parks, food courts, daycare facilities, and other amenities that make daily work more convenient.

Inside the office, the focus is shifting towards collaboration and employee experience. Companies are moving away from traditional hierarchical layouts toward spaces where people can exchange ideas, work , and think differently.

Khedia said businesses are increasingly treating offices as communities that support employees, rather than simply as fixed assets or status symbols.

Bringing offices closer to employees

Location remains important, particularly in large cities such as Bengaluru and Mumbai, where employees may spend two to three hours commuting each day. The time, cost, and effort involved are among the reasons companies are exploring hybrid working arrangements and the hub-and-spoke model.

Instead of operating from one central office, businesses can set up workspaces in different locations, allowing employees to work closer to home.

Khedia said the aim is to make time spent in the office more productive while reducing the burden of commuting. Employees have more time for themselves, while companies can provide spaces where teams can collaborate.

The shift is not limited to metropolitan cities. Khedia pointed to Ahmedabad, Kochi, and Coimbatore as emerging business hubs, supported by growing talent pools and improving infrastructure.

India’s expanding Global Capability Centre (GCC) ecosystem is also influencing office requirements. Companies are considering not only where talent is available but also whether a location has the infrastructure employees need to work effectively.

Khedia highlighted the quality of India’s commercial real estate developments and the amenities available in premium office buildings across the country.

For companies expanding into new markets, the growing network of business locations provides more options to access talent without requiring employees to relocate to major cities.

Why companies are choosing flexible offices

Business uncertainty is also changing how companies plan their real estate requirements.

Traditional office leases often require companies to commit to space for five to 10 years, based on projections of future growth. But as businesses become more agile, such long-term commitments can be difficult to make.

“If any multinationals come to India, they would first have to invest in real estate, thinking of a five-year horizon. Now, flexible office spaces have cut down on those uncertainties. They have ensured the companies can think for the next one or two years,” Khedia said.

Flexible workspaces allow businesses to start with smaller offices, expand, or reduce their space as required, and pay for what they use. This can help them manage real estate costs and allocate more resources to hiring and other business priorities.

Office design is changing as well. Traditional cabins and cubicles are making way for more open layouts that encourage interaction between teams. Companies are also incorporating greenery and biophilic design to make workplaces more comfortable and inviting.

Flexible workspace providers and landlords

Khedia said flexible workspace providers are increasingly working with traditional landlords rather than competing with them. Such partnerships can help property owners attract more tenants by offering businesses different ways to occupy office space.

“The flex office space is a true partner to the landlord. They're not changing the landscape, they're complementing the landlord to create a space which will invite more and more tenants to that building,” he said.

He pointed to the growth of the sector in India. When he began his career, flexible offices accounted for about 1% of overall real estate leasing. By the last financial quarter, that share had reached 23%, he said.

He also noted that flexible workspace absorption in India had increased from around half a million square feet to more than 17–18 million square feet.

Providers such as TEC now offer more than desks and meeting rooms. Businesses can access offices tailored to their requirements, including secure private units within a shared infrastructure.

This allows companies to maintain privacy while benefiting from flexible arrangements and opportunities to network with other businesses in the same building.

For companies entering a new market or expanding their operations, the model also reduces the need to set up and manage every aspect of an office independently.

Enterprise 2.0: Beyond the desk

Khedia believes the next phase of office development will focus more closely on employees' everyday needs.

This could include access to healthcare, childcare, food and other facilities within or near office buildings. Such amenities can make workplaces more convenient while helping businesses attract and retain talent.

For Khedia, Enterprise 2.0 is about moving beyond conventional office layouts to create workplaces that support employees throughout the working day.

As companies reconsider their real estate needs, flexibility, collaboration, and employee experience are becoming important factors in deciding what an office should offer.

item.title: Beyond payments: Where venture capital will flow across Indian fintech over the next 24 months
item.description: India's fintech decade was built on distribution. The next one will be built on infrastructure, advice and intelligence—and capital is already repricing accordingly.
item.content:encoded:
India spent the last ten years solving for reach. UPI, Aadhaar-based onboarding, and the Jan Dhan push put a payment instrument in almost every adult hand, and a generation of companies was built on that distribution. That problem is now largely solved. The harder question—how to serve those hundreds of millions of customers profitably, with products that measurably improve their financial lives—is where the next cycle of venture capital will go.

The funding data already reflects the shift. Indian fintech attracted $3.5 billion across 216 disclosed deals in 2024, and $2.9 billion across 156 deals in 2025 roughly 10% less capital across 27% fewer transactions, according to Fintech Global. This fits fewer, larger cheques into a narrower set of theses. Yet fintech remained the largest sector by funding in 2025 at 22% of all Indian startup capital, and close to 26% in the first half of 2026. Capital is not leaving the sector; it is becoming far more selective about where to park itself.

Three themes stand out as most likely to absorb that capital over the next 24 months.

Financial infrastructure: Rebuilding the core

India's financial institutions are running a modern distribution business on decades-old plumbing. Core banking, lending and policy administration systems at most banks, NBFCs and insurers were built for a branch-led world of batch processing and overnight reconciliation—not for real-time payments at population scale, continuous underwriting, or products assembled on the fly from a dozen data sources. Every new capability gets bolted onto that base, and each addition costs more than the last as the architecture ages.

India’s financial institutions need to upgrade their technology, creating one of the largest infrastructure opportunities in the sector. Most legacy systems were not built for the speed and flexibility institutions now need. The next generation of technology will be cloud-based, modular and API-first, making it easier for different systems to work together. Banks and financial institutions want to launch products in weeks, adjust pricing quickly, and add new data sources or distribution partners without rebuilding their core systems. Much of their existing technology cannot support this.

The opportunity extends beyond core banking systems. Financial institutions also need better tools for compliance, managing AI models and their risks, preventing fraud and money laundering, and protecting against cyber threats. They also need infrastructure that allows non-financial businesses to offer financial products, such as loans, cards and escrow accounts. These capabilities are essential to delivering new financial products while meeting regulatory requirements.

Regulation is making these investments more urgent. Since February 2025, Sebi has held regulated intermediaries responsible for the outputs of AI and machine learning tools they use, including those provided by third parties. In August 2025, the RBI’s FREE-AI committee issued 26 recommendations, followed by draft guidance on model risk management and data governance. Meanwhile, the substantive obligations under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, covering consent, notices and individuals’ data rights, are scheduled to take effect in May 2027. Financial institutions will need to demonstrate that their AI systems and data practices meet these requirements. For many, buying proven technology will be more practical than building it themselves.

For venture investors, this creates an attractive opportunity: businesses can generate recurring revenue from financial institutions, with customer relationships that become harder to replace as their software becomes embedded in day-to-day operations. Investors can also benefit from the growth of financial services technology without needing to predict which consumer-facing brand will win.

A less obvious opportunity lies in India’s Account Aggregator ecosystem. Between March 2025 and May 2026, the number of institutions consuming financial data grew by roughly 66%, crossing 1,000, while the number supplying data remained broadly flat at around 176. Demand for consent-based financial data is growing much faster than supply. Building the infrastructure needed to close this gap could become an important opportunity in its own right.

Wealthtech: The distribution is built, the advice is not

The structural tailwinds are no longer in question.

Mutual fund AUM reached Rs 85.76 lakh crore in July 2026, up from Rs 46.4 lakh crore three years earlier, according to ICRA Analytics.

Sebi’s annual report unique notes that mutual fund investors crossed 6.1 crore, growing 13% in a single financial year, with Tier III cities now accounting for more than half the investor base. Unique demat accounts stand at 12.18 crore, against 3.3 crore in April 2020. Households are visibly rotating: net financial savings rose from 27% of household savings in FY23 to 33% in FY25, and household flows into securities markets more than doubled as a share of GDP, from 0.99% to 2.17%.

But the gap between having an investment account and receiving investment advice is stark, and that is where the opportunity lies. In FY2025-26, 7.2 crore new SIPs were registered and 6.8 crore were discontinued or matured, as per Sebi data.

That is near-total churn. It is not a distribution failure because distribution worked. Rather, it is an advice failure.

The supply side explains why. India has roughly 1,042 Sebi-registered investment adviser entities against nearly 1.99 lakh AMFI-registered mutual fund distributors—about 191 commission-earning distributors for every fee-based adviser, and one adviser for every 58,500 mutual fund investors. Human advice at this ratio cannot reach the mass market, because the unit economics of servicing a Rs 5 lakh portfolio with a human adviser have never worked anywhere.

This is where the account aggregator (AA) framework and AI intersect to make something newly plausible. India’s AA rails had cumulatively fulfilled 493.5 million consents across 314.5 million linked accounts by June 2026, roughly tripling in fifteen months, and now span 16 categories of financial information, including deposits, mutual funds, equities, insurance, pension and GST filings. For the first time, a platform can obtain a consented, machine-readable, near-complete picture of a household's finances. Layer AI over that, and the marginal cost of producing a genuinely personalised recommendation—the kind previously reserved for private banking clients—falls by an order of magnitude.

AI: From feature to franchise

The third theme is the broadest, and the one where discipline matters the most. Almost every fintech firm now claims AI. The distinction worth drawing is between AI as a feature—a chatbot bolted onto an existing product—and AI as the reason the business model works at all.

Three variants look durable. First, consumer financial co-pilots that consolidate saving, investing, borrowing and insurance decisions into one interface. Their viability rests entirely on the AA-plus-AI combination above; without consented data, a co-pilot is a search engine with a friendly tone.

Second, enterprise workflow redesign inside financial institutions. Underwriting, collections, KYC remediation, claims processing, and internal audit are high-volume, rules-dense functions where agentic automation has clear economics and buyers have measurable cost lines to attack.

Third, and perhaps the most underrated, India as a delivery centre for AI-enabled professional services to the world. The IT industry was built on labour arbitrage in software; the same institutional muscle—managed delivery, compliance discipline, client trust at scale—can be pointed at legal review, audit, fund administration and healthcare operations, with AI compressing the cost base rather than headcount expanding it. Given India's incumbent position in global services, this may prove the largest of the three.

What all this adds up to

Payments proved Indians would adopt digital finance. The next 24 months will test whether the ecosystem can make that adoption profitable, well-advised and defensible, which makes a strong case for backing the layers rather than the surfaces: better technology for financial institutions, accessible financial advice for households, and AI that makes both economically possible.

The author is Principal, Flourish Ventures.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: The Indian crypto investor is changing. Is the industry keeping up?
item.description: As India's crypto investor base expands beyond metros and attracts younger, first-time investors, exchanges must look beyond onboarding to education, security and transparency. The piece explores how crypto platforms need to evolve to build trust and serve a more diverse investor base.
item.content:encoded:
When I started building WazirX, making crypto accessible was an immediate challenge. Today, accessibility means much more than opening an account. It means helping someone understand what they own, assess risk, protect their assets and meet their reporting obligations.

The audience is changing. The industry must change how it serves them. Our H1 2026 report found that more than 82% of WazirX users came from non-metro cities. The typical investor was a 34-year-old working professional. Meanwhile, Gen Z accounted for 72% of new investors during the half year. Our International Youth Day report found that nearly 80% of Gen Z users lived outside India's top ten cities.

These are different groups with different needs. A salaried professional building long-term exposure should not have to navigate the same experience as someone learning to place their first order. The Youth Day findings add another responsibility: 44.4% of our Gen Z investors began their investment journey through crypto. For these users, an exchange may also be their first encounter with financial risk.

Our report classified 59% of Gen Z portfolios in utility-focused categories, 25% in established blue-chip crypto and 16% in memecoins. This suggests interests extending beyond the loudest market narratives. It does not establish that every investment is well researched or appropriately sized. These findings describe WazirX users, rather than India's entire market.

What should companies do with this information?

First, build education into the product. Before a first purchase, explain volatility, liquidity and position sizing through short examples in Indian languages. Before a futures order, show how leverage changes potential losses and where liquidation could occur. Offer practice accounts and simple knowledge checks. Measure comprehension, alongside content views.

Second, design around experience and purpose. Let beginners start with a simpler interface, while experienced traders can access advanced tools. Make portfolio concentration visible. Give users clear order previews and accessible controls for managing positions. Growth in futures participation makes these safeguards more urgent. Higher trading activity alone cannot tell us whether users understand their exposure.

Third, make the full cost visible before confirmation. Display trading fees, spreads, estimated slippage and funding costs where applicable. Explain subscription terms and withdrawal charges clearly. A low advertised fee means little if the customer cannot understand the eventual cost of a transaction.

Fourth, make security an operating discipline that users can evaluate. WazirX's cyberattack taught us how deeply failures affect customers. Companies must explain custody arrangements, strengthen transaction approvals, restrict privileged access, assess vendors and rehearse incident response. Publish meaningful security updates and communicate promptly when access is disrupted. A custody partnership is one component of that responsibility.

Fifth, make research and compliance easier. AI assistants can help users compare market information, understand portfolio exposure and prepare questions. They should disclose data limitations, avoid assurances about returns and require confirmation before transactions. Reporting tools should organise transaction histories, provide downloadable records and help users prepare for tax filing. Convenience should strengthen the user's control over decisions.

Sixth, invest in support beyond onboarding. Users in smaller cities deserve understandable answers about deposits, withdrawals and account access. Provide Indian-language assistance, clear escalation routes and realistic resolution timelines. Track resolution quality and recurring complaints, alongside response speed. Product teams should use those complaints to fix underlying problems.

Policy reform remains important. A more proportionate tax framework and consistent obligations across service providers can support participation on compliant Indian platforms. But companies already have considerable work within their control. We should not make better service conditional on regulatory change.

The next phase also requires a broader definition of success. Exchanges should track whether customers understand products, resolve problems successfully and return because the service is dependable. Trading volume matters to a business. It cannot be its only measure of progress.

That means listening to users regularly and making their feedback part of decisions about features, communication, support and overall platform reliability.

I believe India's opportunity lies in the curiosity of people discovering this technology across cities, professions and generations. Our job is to give that curiosity a foundation: useful information, understandable products, reliable systems and accountability when things go wrong.

The Indian crypto investor is asking more of the industry. We should respond by building services worthy of that expectation.

(Nischal Shetty is the Founder of WazirX)

item.title: Ola Electric hands the keys to dealers. What led to this shift in gears?
item.description: For long, Ola Electric ran its own showrooms and sold directly to customers. Now it is shifting to a dealer-led model with plans to have 700 dealer outlets by March 2027. What prompted this reset and what should the company do for it to work?
item.content:encoded:
On November 1, Ola Electric stopped taking orders at its own showrooms. Most of them will be shut by December, as Ola moves away from the direct-to-consumer model that defined the company and turns to a dealer-led business.

Ola has recorded this in its investor presentation filed with the NSE and BSE on November 12 under Regulation 30 of the SEBI Listing Regulations. The document covers the unaudited standalone and consolidated results for the second quarter and half-year ended September 30, 2026.

In its Q2 FY27 shareholders' letter, dated November 12, the company calls the move towards a dealer-led model a "reset". What prompted this 'reset'?

The numbers tell part of the story. Consolidated revenue from operations was Rs 828 crore in Q1 FY26. It fell to Rs 690 crore in Q2, then Rs 470 crore in the next quarter, and bottomed out at Rs 265 crore in Q4 FY26.

Interestingly, the electric two-wheeler market has been growing in recent times. In Q2 FY27, industry volumes reached 5,99,317 units, up 82.7% year on year, and EV penetration in the two-wheeler market touched 11.2%. However, Ola's Q2 revenue fell 39% to Rs 421 crore in FY27.

The service record behind the reset

The shareholders' letter says little about why the direct model had to go, but public records give an indication.

The problems began with service. Between September 2023 and August 2024, the maker of electric two-wheelers received 10,644 complaints through the National Consumer Helpline. Of these, 3,389 concerned service delays and 1,899 were about delayed deliveries, according to media reports.

On October 7, 2024 the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) issued a show-cause notice giving the company 15 days to respond, and the complaints it cited included charges during the free service period, refusals or delays in warranty work, and unsatisfactory repairs.

Ola's response was that 99.1% of the complaints had been resolved to the customer's complete satisfaction. But the regulator reportedly found that 80% of those claimed resolutions had not been implemented, and the CCPA widened its inquiry.

Founder Bhavish Aggarwal promised the backlog would clear soon, and said the company would double its own service network to 1,000 centres by December 2024. Around the same time, a public spat erupted between Aggarwal and the comedian Kunal Kamra, who had taken up the customers' service complaints.

Subsequently, the company-owned store network ran into another problem. In March 2025, Bloomberg reported that only about 100 of Ola's roughly 3,400 showrooms displayed the trade certificate that the Motor Vehicles Act requires. Ola called the report misplaced and prejudiced.

Transport officials raided at least 26 stores in Maharashtra and six in Madhya Pradesh and impounded 60 scooters. Maharashtra's transport minister later said that of 432 stores inspected in April 2025, only 47 held valid certificates, and that the other 385 were shut.

The shareholders' letter does not connect any of this to the move towards a dealer network.

A new front end, built in eight weeks

The first set of dealer outlets became operational on September 4, on Janmashtami. By Diwali, on November 8, Ola says it had appointed 255 dealer partners operating 319 sales outlets. The company is planning about 450 outlets by December 2026 and 700 by March 2027.

Volumes through the new channel have climbed quickly. Wholesale orders were 3,955 vehicles in September and 13,505 in October. Ola expects 16,000 in November and 20,000 in December. Production is meant to keep pace, from 9,235 vehicles in August and 14,092 in October to about 25,000 in December.

The case Ola makes for dealers is financial as much as commercial. Under the old model, the company owned the stores, and carried the stock and the working capital. Now, it says, dealers pay for vehicles when they order them and hold the inventory in their own outlets.

Auto borrowings have fallen from Rs 2,422 crore in December 2024 to Rs 337 crore in September 2026, helped by a QIP and rights issue, and the company expects the auto business to generate free cash flow in the near term.

Operating expenses are meant to fall by a further Rs 50 crore as the company-owned stores close.

What the letter does not hide

The letter is candid in places. Inventory in the dealer channel built up through October and November, and registrations were a little slower in October. Ola puts channel inventory at about 15 days, and under a week in the earliest showrooms. It says that in markets where dealers opened early and have settled in, its market share is now well above pre-transition levels, though the company doe not give any figure.

There is also a supply problem. About 5,000 vehicles with paid orders in September were delayed by a week, running into October, because chargers were unavailable. The company says it is facing a paid order backlog and the constraint is its supply chain, not its plant, which it says can build well above the current output.

Hence the letter's headline claim: demand is no longer the constraint, supply is. The claim deserves attention. Wholesale figures count vehicles sent to dealers, not vehicles sold to riders, and the letter admits slower registrations in October.

The margin trade

Dealers do not come free. Ola says gross margin, which held at about 29.9% in Q2, will dip a little in Q3 and Q4 because of the dealer rollout, while operating margin should improve meaningfully. Excluding PLI incentives, Q2 gross margin was 26.5%. Gross margin per unit was roughly Rs 35,000, against an average selling price of about Rs 1,21,000, down from about Rs 1,68,000 in FY23.

The losses remain large. Operating EBITDA was a loss of Rs 218 crore in Q2FY27, wider than Rs 165 crore in Q1, and the loss after tax was Rs 362 crore. Consolidated free cash flow was negative Rs 371 crore, with the auto segment accounting for Rs 134 crore of that and the cell business most of the rest. Total borrowings are down from Rs 3,132 crore to Rs 1,819 crore.

The product roadmap

Going forward, Ola is betting on two things to win customers back: a cheaper scooter and its own batteries.

The cheaper scooter is the S1Z, which is expected to be delivered to customers by March 2027. It uses a battery type that Ola says costs less to build. The company plans to fit the same battery to its existing models. It also says that, as dealers open, demand will shift towards its premium scooters and motorcycles.

The batteries come from Ola’s own factory, which has reached its first 6 gigawatt-hours of capacity ahead of schedule. The government has extended a production incentive for the plant to 2031, and Ola expects the payments to kick in from January to March.

According to the company, making its own batteries costs the same as buying them, if about 70% of those made pass quality checks, and 10 to 15% less if 85% of them pass checks.

What to watch out for

A company not only owns its product but also owns every complaint that comes with it. While dealers will now share that responsibility, Ola cannot simply wish away all issues with a reset. It has to address the structural challenges that led to the bottlenecks and delays.

The success of the transition hinges on three major factors.

The first is sell-through: whether registrations keep pace with wholesale dispatches as the dealer network grows from 319 outlets to 700. The second is supply: whether production really reaches 25,000 a month, and whether suppliers and chargers keep up with it. The third test is margin: whether the cost savings from closing company showrooms outweigh the gross margin given up to dealers.

Ola has moved quickly, and the early numbers seem to be favourable. But they are the company's own, and they cover only a few weeks. The real proof will come in the Q3 results.

item.title: 5 lessons from The Life That's Waiting by Brianna Wiest
item.description: Discover five meaningful lessons from The Life That's Waiting by Brianna Wiest on self-discovery, emotional healing, happiness, and personal growth.
item.content:encoded:
Sometimes, the life we truly want begins when we stop holding on to the life we think we should have. We spend so much time worrying about the future, comparing ourselves with others, and trying to control every outcome that we forget to enjoy the present.

In The Life That's Waiting, Brianna Wiest explores the idea of creating a life that feels authentic, meaningful, and aligned with who we are becoming. Through reflections on heartbreak, fear, uncertainty, happiness, and personal transformation, she encourages readers to let go of limiting patterns and make room for new possibilities.

The book reminds us that we do not need to have everything figured out to move forward. Sometimes, the smallest decisions can bring us closer to the life we have always wanted.

5 Important lessons to learn from The Life That's Waiting by Brianna Wiest

1. Happiness is built through small daily actions

We often believe that happiness will arrive when we achieve a particular goal, find the right relationship, or reach a certain stage in life. However, constantly waiting for the next big achievement can prevent us from appreciating the present.

Wiest encourages readers to find happiness in small, repeated actions. Taking care of yourself, maintaining meaningful routines, expressing your feelings, and making time for things that matter can gradually create a more fulfilling life.

The lesson is to stop treating happiness as a distant destination and start building it through everyday choices.

2. Let go of what no longer helps you grow

Sometimes, the things that once made us feel comfortable no longer support the people we are becoming. This could be an old relationship, a familiar environment, limiting beliefs, or expectations we have carried for years.

The book reminds readers that outgrowing something does not mean that it was never meaningful. It simply means that different phases of life require different choices.

Allow yourself to move forward without feeling guilty about leaving behind what no longer aligns with your growth.

3. Stop comparing your journey with others

In a world where everyone shares their achievements, milestones, and happiest moments, it is easy to feel that you are falling behind.

However, comparison often distracts us from understanding what we genuinely want. Instead of measuring your success through someone else's timeline, focus on building a life that reflects your own values and priorities.

Wiest encourages readers to reconnect with themselves rather than constantly seeking validation from the outside world.

Remember, you do not have to follow someone else's timeline to create a meaningful life.

4. Your purpose begins with small decisions

Many people believe that finding their purpose requires discovering one extraordinary passion or making a life-changing decision. But purpose does not always arrive as a clear answer.

Sometimes, it begins with small interests, meaningful conversations, creative ideas, or opportunities that make you curious.

The book encourages readers to pay attention to these small signs and take action instead of waiting until they have complete clarity.

You do not need to know exactly where you are going. Sometimes, taking one meaningful step is enough to discover the next.

5. Take small steps even when you feel afraid

Fear often appears when we are about to make an important decision or step into something unfamiliar. It can make us question our abilities and convince us to remain in situations that no longer make us happy.

Wiest encourages readers not to let fear become the reason they stop moving forward. Instead of waiting until you feel completely confident, start with one small action.

Whether it is applying for a new opportunity, starting a project, having a difficult conversation, or making a personal decision, progress begins when you choose to act despite uncertainty.

Final thoughts

The Life That's Waiting by Brianna Wiest is a thoughtful reminder that the life we want to experience often requires us to change the way we think, feel, and make decisions.

Its biggest lesson is that you do not have to wait for the perfect circumstances to begin living meaningfully. Let go of comparison, make peace with change, follow what genuinely inspires you, and take small steps towards the future you want.

Sometimes, the life you have been waiting for begins when you finally permit yourself to live it.

item.title: 5 lessons from Here, There and Everywhere by Sudha Murty
item.description: Discover five meaningful lessons from Here, There and Everywhere by Sudha Murty on kindness, humility, relationships, gratitude, and simple living.
item.content:encoded:
Life's most meaningful lessons often come from ordinary experiences, unexpected encounters, and the people we meet along the way. Sometimes, a simple conversation or a small act of kindness can change the way we understand the world.

In Here, There and Everywhere, Sudha Murty brings together a collection of stories inspired by her experiences and observations of people from different walks of life. Through everyday situations, she explores human relationships, generosity, humility, and the values that make life meaningful.

The book reminds readers that wisdom is not always found in grand achievements. Often, it is hidden in the simplest moments of everyday life.

5 lessons to learn from Here, There and Everywhere by Sudha Murty

1. Kindness can change someone's life

Small acts of kindness can have a lasting impact on people. Sometimes, helping someone does not require wealth or influence; it simply requires empathy and a willingness to understand their situation.

The stories remind us that even a small gesture, such as helping a stranger or supporting someone during a difficult time, can create a meaningful difference.

2. Never judge people by their appearance

We often form opinions about people based on their clothes, financial status, education, or social background. However, appearances rarely reveal someone's true character or circumstances.

The book encourages readers to look beyond outward appearances and treat everyone with dignity and respect.

3. Education builds confidence and independence

Education is not limited to academic qualifications. It also gives people the confidence to express themselves, make informed decisions, and challenge social expectations.

Through stories drawn from different experiences, Murty highlights how learning can open doors, particularly for those who face social and economic barriers.

4. Humility is more valuable than wealth

Success and financial achievements do not automatically make someone a better person. What truly matters is how we treat others, especially those who cannot offer us anything in return.

The book encourages readers to remain humble, regardless of their achievements, and remember that kindness and character are more meaningful than material possessions.

Sudha Murthy’s best quotes on love and relationships

5. Every person has a story worth understanding

We often meet people without knowing what they have experienced or the challenges they have overcome. A stranger's behaviour or circumstances may have a story behind them that we have never considered.

The book reminds us to listen, observe, and approach people with empathy rather than making quick assumptions. Every encounter can teach us something about human nature and life.

Final thoughts

Here, There and Everywhere by Sudha Murty is a collection of stories that finds extraordinary lessons in ordinary experiences. Through encounters with people from different backgrounds, the author explores kindness, courage, education, humility, and human relationships.

The biggest takeaway is that we do not always need extraordinary experiences to learn something valuable. Sometimes, the people we meet and the simplest moments we experience have the most important lessons to offer.

item.title: Credit-led fintech startup Olyv raises $6M
item.description: Founded in 2016 by Rohit Garg, Amit Chandel, Vinay Singh, and Jayant Upadhyay, Olyv offers products across personal loans, gold savings, and credit health management.
item.content:encoded:
Credit-led fintech platform Olyv has raised $6 million (~Rs57 crore) from Nippon Life India AIF Management Limited (Nippon India Alternative Investments) along with existing investors, extending the total Series B funding round to ~$30 million. 

With this investment, Nippon India Alternative Investments joins Olyv’s existing investors including Fundamentum and SMBC Asia Rising Fund. 

Founded in 2016 by Rohit Garg, Amit Chandel, Vinay Singh, and Jayant Upadhyay, Olyv offers products across personal loans, gold savings, and credit health management. 

The company said in a statement that it has nearly 2 million monthly active users and more than 5 crore app downloads, and serves customers across 19,000+ pin codes in India.

Olyv also said it has disbursed ~80 lakh loans and facilitated ~Rs13,000 crore in cumulative transactions, while consistently increasing PAT profitability for 14 consecutive quarters. 

The company is targeting a user base of 100 million and AUM of over $1 billion by By FY29.

Rohit Garg, Co-founder and CEO, Olyv, said, “As we enter our next phase, we are continuing to expand the breadth of our platform, invest in technology and products, and reach the next billion hardworking and underserved consumers with greater financial access and utility.”

The company has so far raised ~$50 million in equity and ~$150 million in debt, from investors including Fundamentum, SMBC Asia Rising Fund, Lightrock, Unicorn India Ventures, and India SME, as well as reputed family offices, including Gauri Khan’s Family Office, and prominent entrepreneurs and sports personalities.

item.title: Oister Global launches Rs 600 Cr deeptech fund
item.description: Oister Global aims to invest in about 8-10 deeptech startups with a proven business model & technology and its capital will assist in rapid scaling.
item.content:encoded:
Oister Global, an India-focused multi-strategy private markets asset manager, has announced the launch of a Rs 600 crore deeptech fund to back revenue generating Indian startups.

The Oister Deep Tech Fund aims to raise Rs 400 crore with a Rs 200 crore greenshoe, taking the potential corpus to Rs 600 crore.

A statement from Oister Global said this deeptech fund will build a concentrated portfolio of 8 to 10 mature companies in the frontier tech ecosystem. The fund will focus in sectors such as space technology, defence and aerospace, semiconductors and electronics, quantum technologies, advanced mobility, advanced materials and energy storage.

The fund’s capital will support production expansion, order execution and commercial adoption of these companies.

On the launch of the new fund, Rohit Bhayana, co-CEO & co-founder, Oister Global, highlighted the need for strategic self-reliance in critical technologies with Indian deeptech startups making significant contributions but there were challenges in growth capital.

“Early-stage investors back the idea, and larger institutions tend to wait until a company is well past its hardest years. The growth stage in between, where technology turns into a business, has had very few committed investors. That is the gap we saw, and it is why we launched the Oister Deep Tech Fund,” Bhayana said.

This fund will focus on companies with proven, de-risked technology and proprietary, defensible IP protected by patents in India and internationally. It will look for companies that are revenue-generating, with multiple revenue streams, customers in domestic and international markets, strong policy support and a clear path to liquidity.

Sandeep Sinha, co-founder & co-CEO, Oister Global, said, “Commercialisation is at the centre of how we invest. We look for clear commercial use cases and real paying customers, not just scientific promise, and our role is to help these companies scale and reach new markets. As more family offices and institutions understand the sector, deep tech will become a mainstream allocation rather than a specialist bet.”

Oister said it has already identified an initial shortlist of few companies across sectors, with further investments to be evaluated as the fund is deployed.

item.title: Former Freshworks executives-founded AI startup Dreamteam raises $53M
item.description: Dreamteam raised this funding from Together Fund, Accel and Premji Invest and this capital will be primarily used to enhance its tech platform
item.content:encoded:
Dreamteam, an AI native customer relationship management (CRM) startup founded by former executives of Freshworks, has raised $53 million in funding from Together Fund, Accel and Premji Invest.

Founded in 2025 by Anand Venkatraman, Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy with headquarters in California and core engineering team in Chennai, is building a technology platform that can understand customer context and have the right AI coworkers to execute.

“The CRM was supposed to give companies a complete picture of their customers, yet the richest parts of that picture have always lived outside the CRM,” said Anand Venkatraman, Co-founder and CEO of Dreamteam.

“AI finally gives us a way to change that foundation. Dreamteam learns from the work your team is already doing, keeps the context alive and gives every salesperson skilled AI teammates that can reason over it and move deals forward. Your sellers and leaders can spend their time on relationships, judgement and closing deals, while Dreamteam takes care of everything required around them,” he said.

According to a statement from Dreamteam, companies across diverse industries, including AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing, and consulting are using their technology platform.

Girish Mathrubootham, Founding partner at Together Fund, the first institutional investor in Dreamteam added: “CRM is among the biggest software categories ripe for disruption. I've worked alongside Dreamteam's founders since day one as their vision for an AI-native CRM took shape. Their deep CRM expertise and proven record of scaling enterprise software make them uniquely positioned to lead this reinvention.”

Looking ahead, Dreamteam aims to extend its intelligence layer beyond sales to the entire customer lifecycle, including prospecting, onboarding, customer success and upselling. The company also offers Magic Apps, which allows business users to create custom applications and dashboards using natural language without writing code.

Shekhar Kirani, Partner at Accel said, “In the AI era, the companies that understand their customers deeply have an enormous advantage. Today, everyone on a team sees a different version of the customer, because no central system holds all the information. Dreamteam is building that system with AI agents.”

item.title: upGrad broadens its business with new workforce advisory venture
item.description: upGrad launches workforce advisory business as it expands beyond skilling, aiming to help organisations navigate AI-led transformation through integrated workforce strategy and implementation.
item.content:encoded:
Edtech firm upGrad has launched upGrad Next, a workforce advisory business intended to help organisations redesign how they structure, hire, reward and develop employees as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes work.

The move broadens upGrad’s corporate offering as it diversifies beyond skilling into higher education, professional courses, study-abroad services and enterprise learning. Its acquisition of Unacademy adds competitive exam preparation to its edtech portfolio, as the company, led by chairperson and co-founder Ronnie Screwvala, eyes a potential IPO.

Anandorup Ghose will lead Next as managing director, with Hrishikesh Godbole, Krishna Chaitanya and Dinkar Pawan among the initial team.

Screwvala described the launch as a response to the next phase of digital change. “The last decade, in many ways, was about the complete digital transformation of organisations. We see the next decade being about transforming the workforce to manage, and get strong returns from, the change that has already happened.” 

Next will advise on organisational structure, recruitment, pay and workforce development, and help put those decisions into practice. upGrad said it will combine experienced advisers with AI and its skilling and hiring operations, with accountability for outcomes rather than consultant time billed.

Ghose, who has spent more than 24 years in HR and rewards consulting, worked as a partner at Aon and Deloitte and led the latter’s rewards consulting practice globally. He sees a gap between large technology transformation programmes and specialist products. “These demand experience and judgment. The next decade won't be won by those who adopt technology fastest, but by those who unlock human potential most effectively.”

His argument is that decisions about AI investment, job design and employee capability need to be made together. Technology adoption alone does not guarantee higher productivity.

Aon’s 2026 Human Capital Trends study found that 43% of organisations in India had deployed AI and a further 20% were piloting it, but translating investment into workforce outcomes remained difficult. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 estimated that 39% of workers’ existing skill sets would be transformed or become outdated by 2030, while 63% of employers saw skills gaps as a major barrier to business transformation.

Consulting and technology firms are also combining these capabilities. In October 2026, KPMG in India and HR technology company PeopleStrong announced an alliance pairing workforce advice with AI-enabled human capital management software for employee data and HR processes. In September, Deloitte launched an Open Model Engineering practice to help organisations build and deploy AI tools for business use, and said it would hire and train specialists to work alongside clients. Both moves highlight the growing overlap between advice and implementation.

Meanwhile, the Government programmes are expanding the skills pipeline. The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship said the Skill India Digital Hub’s SOAR programme now includes 50 AI and AI-application qualifications. By August 2026, more than 517,000 learners had enrolled and over 100,000 had been certified.

item.title: Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset; Menopause in India’s public health agenda
item.description: The company is betting on a cheaper S1Z scooter and in-house battery manufacturing to win back customers, though the long-term success of its reset depends on retail registrations, supply chain stability, and margin recovery.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

India’s deeptech ecosystem just got a major capital boost. Multi-strategy asset manager Oister Global has launched the Oister Deep Tech Fund, targeting up to Rs 600 crore to back revenue-generating Indian startups. The fund will build a concentrated portfolio of eight to ten mature companies in the frontier tech ecosystem.

Meanwhile, upGrad has launched upGrad Next, a workforce advisory business that will help organisations redesign how they structure, hire, reward and develop employees amid workplace changes due to AI. The move expands upGrad’s corporate offering as it moves beyond skilling into higher education, professional courses, study-abroad services and enterprise learning.

In other news, India’s deeptech companies raised $914 million in 257 rounds in 2025, 34 times the 2016 level. The harder test is turning research and prototypes into commercial products, according to Speciale Invest’s report, India’s Deep Tech Revolution - From the Lab to Growth and Exits.

Edtech companies aren’t the only ones betting big on AI learning. Government programmes are also rapidly expanding India's talent pipeline. According to the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, the Skill India Digital Hub’s SOAR programme now offers 50 AI and AI-application qualifications, drawing over 517,000 enrolments and certifying more than 100,000 learners as of August 2026.

Elsewhere, a new kind of revolution is brewing. About 3.76 crore rural women belonging to self-help groups have achieved Lakhpati Didi status. The Centre’s rural livelihood initiative aims to create 6 crore Lakhpati Didis by March 2029. Additionally, 5.70 crore women have been identified as Potential Lakhpati Didis.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset
  • Menopause in India’s public health agenda

Here’s your trivia for today: Which global payments giant began in 1966 when a group of California banks formed the ‘Interbank Card Association’? (Scroll down for the answer)

Analysis

Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset

EV company Ola Electric is abandoning its direct-to-consumer model and shutting most company-owned showrooms by December 2026 to transition into a dealer-led business. While the broader electric two-wheeler market grew significantly, Ola’s revenue dropped sharply amid severe service backlogs, consumer complaints, and regulatory store closures over missing trade certificates. To recover, Ola rapidly established over 319 dealer outlets, shifting inventory costs to partners and boosting wholesale orders.

Key takeaways:

  • The company is betting on a cheaper S1Z scooter and in-house battery manufacturing to win back customers, though the long-term success of its reset depends on retail registrations, supply chain stability, and margin recovery.
  • The company's Q2 FY27 revenue dropped by 39% to Rs 421 crore even as the wider electric two-wheeler market grew.
  • Between September 2023 and August 2024, the maker of electric two-wheelers received 10,644 complaints through the National Consumer Helpline. Of these, 3,389 concerned service delays and 1,899 were about delayed deliveries, according to media reports.

Health and wellbeing

Menopause in India’s public health agenda

Millions of women in India navigate menopause with little to no support from family or even their healthcare providers. That’s why the Karnataka government’s recent order for a three-month pilot of Ruthu Taare, its Mid-Life Women’s Health and Menopause Programme, in Dakshina district is a welcome step in the right direction.

Key takeaways:

  • The programme will feature dedicated clinics, comprehensive health screenings, mental health assessments, nutrition counselling, and referrals for women aged 35 and above.
  • The pilot will organise dedicated clinic sessions every Wednesday at primary health centres, taluka and district hospitals. Designated medical colleges may organise special clinics on Saturdays.
  • The Ruthu Taare initiative is important because it attempts to bring menopausal care into mainstream conversation and integrate it into public healthcare.

The class-action complaint follows a grim financial forecast that sent Intel's stock plunging nearly 29% in a single day, wiping out roughly $140 billion in market value.
  • Charity: Warren Buffett has announced that he is donating roughly $5.47 billion in Berkshire Hathaway shares to four charities led by his adult children. Accompanying his annual Thanksgiving gift, the legendary investor stated that his confidence in the conglomerate he built over six decades remains “as strong as ever.”
